title: why the symbol is an execution device
hookLine: why the symbol is an execution device
carry: the worst thing is not the last thing
tomorrow: the women went to the tomb first

lines: ON A STEEPLE. ON A NECKLACE.
NOW SWAP IN AN ELECTRIC CHAIR.
cards: On a steeple. On a necklace. Tattooed on a forearm.
Hanging from a rearview mirror. The cross is everywhere, and it's easy to stop seeing it. So try a swap.
A movement whose symbol was an electric chair. A tiny gold noose on a chain. It sounds unthinkable.
But that's what the cross was to the people who first saw it: the way Rome killed the people it wanted everyone to watch die. So why would anyone wear one?

teach.b: Crucifixion was how Rome executed slaves, rebels and anyone it saw as a threat to order. It was slow, and it was public on purpose.

The Gospels say Jesus was arrested at night, questioned, and handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, who sentenced him. Roman soldiers carried it out. Over his head was written the charge: the King of the Jews.
A mockery, and a warning. The Gospels keep a few things he said there.
One has him pray: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." In Mark's Gospel he cries out, in his own language, yesterday's line: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
The Gospels don't smooth that over. Some Christian readers say it's there so that anyone who has felt abandoned knows he felt it too. Then a turn in the history.

Historians of early Christian art say the oldest surviving images more often show other signs: a fish, an anchor, a shepherd. The cross became the main symbol later, after Rome stopped crucifying people.
Christians say something happened there that changed what the worst thing means. Churches put it in different words: a sacrifice, a rescue, love going all the way down. And they show it differently.
Catholic and Orthodox churches often show the crucifix, with Jesus on it.

teach.h: THE CRUCIFIX AND THE EMPTY CROSS.
teach.b: Some Protestant churches show the cross empty.
Both are saying something about that Friday: it happened, and Christians say it wasn't the end.

how: Christians remember the crucifixion on Good Friday, the Friday before Easter. Catholic, Orthodox and some Protestant Christians make the sign of the cross when they pray, and churches often hold a crucifix or a plain cross at the front.

s: the cross was Christianity's main symbol from day one
historians say the oldest surviving Christian images more often show a fish, an anchor or a shepherd.
Rome crucified people in public on purpose
it was meant to be seen. a punishment and a warning to everyone passing by.
in Mark, Jesus cries out the first line of a psalm
"my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" it's the opening of Psalm 22, yesterday's line.

games.q: the soldiers have nailed him up and are gambling for his clothes. in one Gospel, what does Jesus say about them?
o: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
games.why: Luke puts both in one verse: the prayer for the soldiers, and the soldiers dividing his clothes.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out. Think of a hard thing from this year.
Not the hardest. Just name it, quietly, without reliving it. Now notice one plain fact: you're still here.
Something came after it, even if it's only this minute, sitting and breathing. You don't have to make it mean anything. Just hold both: it happened, and it wasn't the last thing.
If you pray, you can bring it with you.
